o: It encrypts an object for secure storage
It converts an in-memory object into a string representation that can be stored or transmitted
It compresses objects to reduce cookie size
It validates object properties against a schema
questions.x: Serialization captures the state of an object as a string. The reverse operation, deserialization, reconstructs the object from that string. PHP uses serialize() and unserialize() for this.
questions.h: Think of it as taking a snapshot of an object in memory and turning it into text. What would the reverse operation be called?

questions.q: Which PHP function is at the core of this vulnerability?
o: json_decode()
unserialize()
base64_decode()
eval()
questions.x: unserialize() reconstructs a PHP object from a string. If that string is user-controlled and the codebase contains classes with dangerous magic methods, the attacker can inject an object of any available class.
questions.h: The vulnerability is called insecure deserialization. What is the PHP function that performs deserialization?

questions.q: What is a PHP magic method?
o: A method that requires admin privileges to call
A special method that PHP calls automatically at defined lifecycle points, such as object creation or destruction
A method that encrypts its return value automatically
A method only accessible through reflection
questions.x: Magic methods have double-underscore names like __construct(), __destruct(), __wakeup(). PHP calls them automatically at specific moments, not when you explicitly invoke them.
questions.h: These methods start with __ and PHP calls them without you writing an explicit function call. When in an object's life do you think they fire?

questions.q: Why is __destruct() particularly useful in a deserialization exploit?
o: It runs when the object is first created, allowing code injection on deserialization
It runs when the object is garbage-collected after use, executing attacker-controlled logic without any explicit call
It encrypts the object before it is destroyed
It is called when the session ends, making it useful for persistence
questions.x: PHP calls __destruct() automatically when an object goes out of scope. If the class has dangerous code there, such as deleting a file or running a command, it executes just by deserializing an object of that class.
questions.h: dest- in __destruct hints at the lifecycle moment. When is an object destroyed? And does the attacker need to call this method explicitly?

questions.q: How was the malicious serialized payload delivered to the server in this lab?
o: As a URL query parameter
As the session cookie value
As a POST body JSON field
As a custom HTTP header
questions.x: PHP applications often store serialized session data in a cookie. Replacing the cookie with a crafted serialized object is the standard injection vector for this class of attack.
questions.h: PHP session data is often stored somewhere that travels with every HTTP request. Where does a browser automatically send stored session data?

questions.q: What did the backup file expose that made the exploit possible?
o: The admin password in plain text
The PHP class definition including its properties and magic methods, revealing the gadget
The server's private SSH key
The database connection string
questions.x: Source code access via the backup file (CustomTemplate.php~) revealed the class name, its properties, and the dangerous logic in __destruct(). Without this, crafting a working payload would be guessing.
questions.h: To craft a serialized object for a specific class, you need to know the class name, its property names, and what code runs automatically. Where did the writeup find all that?

questions.q: In PHP serialization format, what does O:14:"CustomTemplate":1:{...} mean?
o: An array with 14 elements inside CustomTemplate
An object of the class CustomTemplate, where 14 is the class name length and 1 is the property count
A base64 value of length 14 wrapped in a custom template
An error code object with ID 14
questions.x: PHP serialization uses O:<name_length>:"<class>":<property_count>:{<properties>}. O stands for Object. The number after O is the byte length of the class name string, not an ID.
questions.h: Break down the format: the letter, the number after it, the quoted string, then another number. What does each position represent?

questions.q: What is a 'gadget' in the context of PHP deserialization?
o: A Burp Suite extension for generating payloads
An existing class in the codebase with a magic method that performs a dangerous operation the attacker can trigger
A PHP function that bypasses serialization restrictions
A specially crafted cookie prefix
questions.x: A gadget is a class already present in the application or its dependencies that contains a magic method with dangerous behavior. The attacker does not introduce new code, just instantiates an existing dangerous class.
questions.h: The attacker does not inject PHP code as text. They inject an object of a class that already exists. What makes a class useful as a gadget?

questions.q: What was the dangerous operation performed by the __destruct() method of the exploited class?
o: Executing a shell command
Deleting a file using the object's lock_file_path property
Sending an HTTP request to an external server
Writing to a log file
questions.x: The __destruct() method called unlink() on the lock_file_path property. By setting that property to /home/carlos/morale.txt in the serialized payload, the attacker triggered file deletion when the object was destroyed.
questions.h: The lab goal is to delete a specific file. What PHP function deletes a file, and where in the class would you expect to find it being called automatically?

questions.q: What is the most direct fix for insecure deserialization?
o: Encrypt the serialized data before storing it in a cookie
Never pass user-controlled data to unserialize(), and use safer formats like JSON for data exchange
Add HMAC integrity checking to cookies
Disable all magic methods in PHP classes
questions.x: unserialize() with user input is inherently dangerous regardless of filtering. The correct fix is to not use PHP serialization for user-controlled data and instead use JSON or another format that does not reconstruct arbitrary objects.
questions.h: HMAC signing helps but does not fully close the attack surface if the secret leaks. What is the more fundamental fix that removes the deserialization surface entirely?
